questions.stem: A function f is a probability density function on [a, b] when:
options: f(x) ≤ 1 on [a, b] and the integral of f from a to b is 1
f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b] and f(b) − f(a) = 1
f(a) = 0, f(b) = 1 and f is increasing on [a, b]
f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b] and the integral of f from a to b is 1
questions.explanation: A density cannot be negative, and the total area under it must be 1 because it covers every possible value. A density can exceed 1 at some points, as f(x) = 2x does near x = 1, as long as the total area is 1.

questions.stem: X is a continuous random variable. What is Pr(X = 2)?
questions.explanation: For a continuous random variable, probability is area under the density curve, and the area above a single point is 0. The value f(2) is the height of the density, which is not a probability.

questions.stem: The standard normal random variable Z ~ N(0, 1) has:
questions.explanation: N(μ, σ²) lists the mean and the variance, so N(0, 1) has mean 0 and variance 1, and a standard deviation of √1 = 1. Every normal variable can be converted to Z with Z = (X − μ)/σ.

questions.stem: For Z ~ N(0, 1), Pr(Z < −1.5) is equal to:
questions.explanation: The standard normal curve is symmetric about 0, so the area to the left of −1.5 equals the area to the right of 1.5. Pr(Z < 1.5) is the much larger area, about 0.93.

questions.stem: In a survey of 500 Victorian voters, 56% supported a proposal. The value 56% is:
questions.explanation: It is calculated from the 500 people sampled, so it is a statistic, used to estimate the unknown population proportion. The population parameter is the proportion of all Victorian voters, which the survey cannot observe.

questions.stem: Why does the sample proportion vary from one random sample to another?
options: The sample size changes each time a sample is taken.
Each sample is measured with a different confidence level.
Different random samples contain different individuals.
The population proportion changes with every sample.
questions.explanation: The population proportion p is fixed; the sample proportion is a random variable because each sample happens to include different members of the population. That variation is what the sampling distribution describes.

questions.stem: Which value of z is used for an approximate 95% confidence interval for a population proportion?
questions.explanation: Pr(−1.96 < Z < 1.96) ≈ 0.95, so z = 1.96 leaves 2.5% in each tail. The value 1.645 gives a 90% interval and 2.58 gives a 99% interval.

questions.stem: f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, and 0 elsewhere, is a probability density function. What is k?
questions.explanation: The total area must be 1: the integral of kx from 0 to 2 is 2k, so k = 1/2. The value 1/4 comes from integrating x as 2² rather than 2²/2.

questions.stem: For X ~ N(μ, σ²), changing μ while keeping σ fixed:
options: makes the graph wider or narrower
reflects the graph in the y-axis
slides the graph left or right
changes the height of the peak
questions.explanation: The mean is the centre of symmetry, so changing it slides the bell curve left or right. The width and the height of the peak are set by σ alone.

questions.stem: Of 400 randomly chosen households, 120 own a dog. What is the sample proportion?
questions.explanation: The sample proportion is the number with the characteristic divided by the sample size: 120/400 = 0.3. Dividing the other way gives 3.33, which is larger than 1 and cannot be a proportion.

questions.stem: X ~ Bi(n, p) and the sample proportion is X/n. What is the mean of X/n?
questions.explanation: E(X/n) = E(X)/n = np/n = p, so the sample proportion is centred on the population proportion. The value np is the mean of X, the count, before dividing by n.

questions.stem: X has the uniform density f(x) = 1/4 for 2 ≤ x ≤ 6, and 0 elsewhere. What is Pr(X > 5)?
questions.explanation: The probability is the area of the rectangle from 5 to 6, which is 1 × 1/4 = 1/4. The value 3/4 is Pr(X < 5).

questions.stem: For X ~ N(μ, σ²), Pr(μ − σ < X < μ + σ) is approximately:
questions.explanation: About 68% of a normal distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. The value 0.5 is the probability of being on one side of the mean.

questions.stem: f(x) = 3x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and 0 elsewhere. What is E(X)?
questions.explanation: E(X) is the integral of x f(x) = 3x³ from 0 to 1, which is 3/4. The value 1/2 is the midpoint of the interval, which is the mean only for a symmetric density.

questions.stem: f(x) = 3x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and 0 elsewhere. What is Pr(X < 1/2)?
questions.explanation: Pr(X < 1/2) is the integral of 3x² from 0 to 1/2, which is (1/2)³ = 1/8. The value 3/4 is f(1/2), a height, not an area.

questions.stem: f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and 0 elsewhere. What is the median of X?
questions.explanation: The median m satisfies the integral of 2x from 0 to m equal to 1/2, so m² = 1/2 and m = 1/√2 = √2/2 ≈ 0.71. The value 2/3 is the mean, which is not the same as the median for a skewed density.

questions.stem: f(x) = 2e^(−2x) for x ≥ 0, and 0 elsewhere. What is Pr(X > 1)?
questions.explanation: Pr(X > 1) is the integral of 2e^(−2x) from 1 to ∞, which is [−e^(−2x)] = 0 − (−e^(−2)) = e^(−2). The value 1 − e^(−2) is Pr(X < 1).

questions.stem: X ~ N(50, 4²). Using the 68–95–99.7% rule, Pr(X > 58) is approximately:
questions.explanation: 58 is two standard deviations above the mean, and about 95% lies within two standard deviations, leaving 5% split equally between the tails. So the upper tail is about 0.025, not 0.05.

questions.stem: Heights are distributed as X ~ N(170, 8²) cm. Pr(X < 162) is equal to:
questions.explanation: Standardise: z = (162 − 170)/8 = −1. Dividing by the variance 64 or not dividing at all gives the wrong z-value; the difference −8 is measured in units of σ = 8.

questions.stem: For X ~ N(μ, σ²), increasing σ while keeping μ fixed makes the graph:
questions.explanation: A larger standard deviation spreads the values further from the mean, and since the total area stays 1 the peak must come down. The centre stays at μ.

questions.stem: For Z ~ N(0, 1), Pr(Z > a) = 0.2. What is Pr(−a < Z < a)?
questions.explanation: By symmetry Pr(Z < −a) = 0.2 as well, so the middle area is 1 − 0.2 − 0.2 = 0.6. The value 0.8 is Pr(Z < a), which only removes the upper tail.

questions.stem: X is normally distributed and Pr(X > 80) = Pr(X < 40). What is the mean of X?
questions.explanation: A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, so equal tail areas must sit at equal distances from it. The mean is midway between 40 and 80, which is 60.

questions.stem: The population proportion is p = 0.4 and samples of size n = 100 are taken. The mean and standard deviation of the sample proportion are:
questions.explanation: The mean is p = 0.4 and the standard deviation is √(p(1 − p)/n) = √(0.24/100) = √0.0024 ≈ 0.049. The values 40 and √24 describe the count X, not the proportion X/n.

questions.stem: Which change makes the distribution of the sample proportion closer to normal?
questions.explanation: For large samples the distribution of the sample proportion is approximately normal, and the approximation improves as n grows. A value of p near 0 makes it more skewed, and a confidence level has no effect on the distribution itself.

questions.stem: Roughly how must the sample size change to halve the width of an approximate 95% confidence interval for p?
questions.explanation: The width is proportional to 1/√n, so halving it needs √n to double, which means n is multiplied by 4. Doubling n only reduces the width by a factor of √2.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 400 people, the sample proportion is 0.5. An approximate 95% confidence interval for p is:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation estimate is √(0.5 × 0.5/400) = 0.025, and 1.96 × 0.025 = 0.049, so the interval is 0.5 ± 0.049. Leaving out the 1.96 gives (0.475, 0.525), and doubling the margin gives (0.402, 0.598).

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for a population proportion p is calculated from a random sample. The correct interpretation is:
options: about 95% of the population has values that lie inside this interval
about 95% of repeated sample proportions would equal this sample proportion
about 95% of this sample lies inside the interval
about 95% of intervals made this way from repeated samples would contain p
questions.explanation: The confidence level describes the method: if many samples were taken and an interval built from each, about 95% of the intervals would capture the fixed value p. The interval is about a proportion, not about individual values in the population or the sample.

questions.stem: A simulation draws 1000 random samples of size 50 from a population with p = 0.3. The 1000 sample proportions:
options: cluster around 0.3, with fewer far from it
questions.explanation: The sample proportion has mean p = 0.3 and standard deviation √(0.21/50) ≈ 0.065, so most values fall within about 0.13 of 0.3. Random sampling means they cannot all equal 0.3.

questions.stem: One hundred approximate 95% confidence intervals for p are calculated from 100 independent random samples. How many would you expect to miss p?
options: none, because each is centred on p
questions.explanation: Each interval has about a 5% chance of missing p, so about 5 of 100 will, but the actual count is random. The intervals are centred on their own sample proportions, not on p, which is why some miss it.

questions.stem: Changing from an approximate 95% to an approximate 99% confidence interval from the same sample makes the interval:
questions.explanation: A 99% interval uses z ≈ 2.58 instead of 1.96, so the margin of error is larger. Being more confident of capturing p requires a wider net.

questions.stem: An approximate 95% confidence interval for p is (0.32, 0.48). What was the sample proportion?
questions.explanation: The interval is symmetric about the sample proportion, so it is the midpoint: (0.32 + 0.48)/2 = 0.40. The value 0.08 is the margin of error and 0.16 is the width.

questions.stem: f(x) = k(4 − x²) for −2 ≤ x ≤ 2, and 0 elsewhere, is a probability density function. What is k?
questions.explanation: The integral of 4 − x² from −2 to 2 is 2(8 − 8/3) = 32/3, so k × 32/3 = 1 and k = 3/32. Integrating only from 0 to 2 gives 16/3 and the wrong value 3/16.

questions.stem: A continuous random variable X has standard deviation 2. What is the standard deviation of 3X + 1?
questions.explanation: sd(aX + b) = |a| sd(X) = 3 × 2 = 6, because adding 1 does not change the spread. The value 36 is Var(3X + 1) = 9 × 4.

questions.stem: f(x) = 3x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and 0 elsewhere. What is Var(X)?
questions.explanation: E(X²) is the integral of 3x⁴ from 0 to 1, which is 3/5, and E(X) = 3/4, so Var(X) = 3/5 − 9/16 = 3/80. Subtracting E(X) instead of its square gives −3/20, and a variance cannot be negative.

questions.stem: f(x) = (1/2)sin(x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ π, and 0 elsewhere. What is Pr(X < π/3)?
questions.explanation: The integral of (1/2)sin(x) from 0 to π/3 is (1/2)[−cos(x)] = (1/2)(1 − 1/2) = 1/4. The value √3/4 is f(π/3), the height of the density there.

questions.stem: f(x) = 2e^(−2x) for x ≥ 0, and 0 elsewhere. What is Pr(X > 2 | X > 1)?
questions.explanation: Pr(X > 2) = e^(−4) and Pr(X > 1) = e^(−2), and since X > 2 already implies X > 1, the conditional probability is e^(−4)/e^(−2) = e^(−2). The value e^(−4) ignores the condition.

questions.stem: X is normal with mean 100 and Pr(X > 110) = 0.025. Using Pr(Z > 1.96) = 0.025, the standard deviation of X is:
questions.explanation: The value 110 must be 1.96 standard deviations above the mean, so 1.96σ = 10 and σ = 10/1.96 ≈ 5.1. Multiplying instead of dividing gives σ ≈ 19.6, which would put 110 only half a standard deviation above the mean.

questions.stem: X ~ N(20, σ²) and Pr(X > 25) = 0.1. What is Pr(X > 25 | X > 20)?
questions.explanation: Pr(X > 20) = 0.5 by symmetry, and X > 25 already implies X > 20, so the conditional probability is 0.1/0.5 = 0.2. Leaving it as 0.1 ignores the condition.

questions.stem: A company claims 52% of customers are satisfied. A random sample gives an approximate 95% confidence interval of (0.42, 0.50). Which conclusion is appropriate?
options: 0.52 lies outside the interval, so the sample gives reason to doubt the claim.
0.52 lies outside the interval, so the claim has been proven false.
0.52 lies outside the interval, but intervals cannot be used to judge claims.
0.52 lies inside the interval, so the sample supports the claim.
questions.explanation: A claimed value outside a 95% interval is not consistent with the sample, so there is evidence against the claim. It is not proof, because about 5% of such intervals miss the true value.

questions.stem: An approximate 95% confidence interval for p has sample proportion 0.4 and margin of error 0.08. Using z = 1.96, what was the sample size?
questions.explanation: Solve 1.96√(0.4 × 0.6/n) = 0.08: √(0.24/n) = 0.0408, so 0.24/n ≈ 0.001666 and n ≈ 144. The value 12 is √144, from stopping before squaring.

questions.stem: Random samples of size 4 are taken from a population with p = 0.5. What is the probability that the sample proportion is 0.75?
questions.explanation: A sample proportion of 0.75 means X = 3 where X ~ Bi(4, 0.5), and Pr(X = 3) = C(4, 3)(0.5)⁴ = 4/16 = 1/4. For a sample this small the normal approximation would be poor, so the binomial is used exactly.

questions.stem: For a continuous random variable with density f on [0, 4], the integral of f from 0 to 1 is 0.3 and the integral from 0 to 3 is 0.8. What is Pr(X > 1 | X < 3)?
questions.explanation: Pr(1 < X < 3) = 0.8 − 0.3 = 0.5 and Pr(X < 3) = 0.8, so the conditional probability is 0.5/0.8 = 5/8. The value 1/2 is the unconditional Pr(1 < X < 3).
